title: How can areas help us find a missing side?
description: Four rectangles with areas twenty eight, twenty one, thirty five and fourteen square inches fit together. Dividing each area by the side that is known gives the missing sides one after another, and the last one is checked by multiplying back.
teaching_notes: One idea: since area is length times width, a missing side is the area divided by the side we know. Watch for children who add the area and the side instead of dividing.

source: Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 1)
video_script.why: The child uses area equals length times width backwards, dividing an area by a known side to find the missing side.
video_script.substitution: Work from the rectangle whose area and one side are known, then use each new side in the next rectangle.
video_script.anchor: the figure of the book made of four rectangles with areas given in square inches
video_script.payoff_line: the width of the fourteen square inch rectangle is two inches
hold_back: the width of the 14 in² rectangle is 2 in
never_show: the width of the 14 in² rectangle, before the answer beat
maths_rules: 21 in² piece is 7 in long: height 21 ÷ 7 = 3 in
28 in² piece is 4 + 3 = 7 in tall: width 28 ÷ 7 = 4 in
35 in² piece is 3 + 4 = 7 in wide: height 35 ÷ 7 = 5 in
14 in² piece is 5 + 2 = 7 in tall: width 14 ÷ 7 = 2 in
video_script.design: One idea: a missing side is the area divided by the known side. The four rectangles stay on stage; each new side is written on the figure as it is found.
open_questions: The figure is not in the extracted book text, so the layout (which edge is shared with which piece) follows the worklist steps and could not be checked against the picture; the label 2 in also appears in the book text, so the worklist may have read the unknown side wrongly.

The second figure of the book question (29 m² and 11 m² pieces, total 50 m²) is not solved here because the worklist reading (lower height 84/29 m) looks doubtful: if 50 m² is the whole rectangle, the top widths 7.25 m and 2.75 m add to 10 m and the lower piece is 1 m tall.
